> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Scope: this is a kernel-level microbenchmark, not an end-to-end throughput claim.**
> Against a multi-millisecond decode step a change of this size sits inside
> run-to-run variation (~1% on a conc=1 arm), so **no measurable serving
> throughput improvement is claimed, and none should be inferred.** The value is
> removing work from a path that is on the critical path at low concurrency.

> [!NOTE]
> **This PR changed approach after review.** It originally split the padding into
> a second kernel to parallelise it across the grid. @okorzh-amd measured that
> the split cost more host time than it saved on device, and identified the real
> cause of the original slowness. The implementation below is her one-launch
> variant. The earlier description, and its 35.8 us figure derived from a kernel
> that no longer exists, have been replaced.

## Purpose

`_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` pads the unused tail of the draft-input buffers so CUDA-graph replay at a larger captured size never reads stale state or writes KV. That padding runs inside the main kernel, guarded on `req_idx == num_reqs - 1`, as serial loops whose trip counts come from the **buffer capacities**, not from the batch:

```python
for i in range(q_pad_start, max_num_tokens, BLOCK_SIZE):
    block = i + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    tl.store(out_query_slot_mapping_ptr + block, PAD_SLOT_ID, mask=block < max_num_tokens)
```

`num_reqs * num_query_per_req` stays small, so that span is essentially `max_num_tokens` at **any** concurrency, and it scales the wrong way: doubling `max_num_batched_tokens` doubles the work for identical real input.

## The actual cause: block width, not serialisation

The loops reuse the **main kernel's** `BLOCK_SIZE`, which is

```python
BLOCK_SIZE = min(256, triton.next_power_of_2(max(1, max_tokens_per_req)))
```

At decode `max_tokens_per_req` is `k+1`, so **8** at spec 7. Walking a 16384-token span 8 elements at a time is **2048 iterations**:

| `max_num_batched_tokens` | BLOCK_SIZE 8 | PAD_BLOCK_SIZE 1024 |
|---|---|---|
| 8192 | 1024 iterations | 8 |
| 16384 | **2048 iterations** | **16** |
| 32768 | 4096 iterations | 32 |

A single program running 16 iterations is not a problem; one running 2048 is. That is where the time went — not from the work being confined to one workgroup.

## The change

Give the padding loops their own `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE` constexpr, sized from the padded span and capped at 1024, instead of inheriting the main kernel's decode-sized width. The padding stays in `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel`, now under `req_idx == num_reqs - 1 and block_idx == 0` (the main grid is 2-D, so without the second term every block of the last request would redo the padding).

No extra launch. That matters here because `prepare_dflash_inputs` is called from the per-draft-KV-group loop in `propose()`, so any added launch repeats per group per step, and K3 decode at conc 1 is sync-bound on host dispatch (#58381).

## Measurement

In situ, Kimi-K3 decode, conc 1, MI355X, `max_num_batched_tokens=16384`, PyTorch profiler trace — the baseline this PR targets:

| | |
|---|---|
| `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` | **38.0 us/step** |
| samples | 48 (6 per step x 8 ranks) |
| min / max | 37.2 / 38.9 us |

**Measurements of the implemented variant are @okorzh-amd's**, on MI355X at spec 7 / 16384 tokens, per call (device / host us):

| | device | host | total |
|---|---|---|---|
| base | 65 | 31.8 | 96.8 |
| second-kernel split (earlier revision, **not** this PR) | 4.4 | 45.3 | 49.7 |
| **this PR — wide block, one launch** | **6.0** | **31.4** | **37.4** |

The split bought 1.6 us of device time for ~13.5 us of host time. The wide block recovers ~97% of the device win with host time unchanged, and is ~12 us better in total. It also avoids the prefill device regression the split caused (5.2 -> 7.7 us).

I have not re-measured the reworked version myself; the numbers above for it are hers.

## Correctness

The padding exists for CUDA-graph safety, so this was checked by simulating both versions' writes and comparing buffers elementwise rather than by arguing from the code.

- Earlier split revision: 900 configurations, 0 mismatches.
- **This revision**: the span-sized width against the original main-`BLOCK_SIZE` form, **468 shapes x 4 block widths x 9 buffers, elementwise, 0 mismatches**. Width changes how many iterations run, not what lands.
- The store set — buffer and value for all 9 buffers — diffs clean against the pre-PR block. The buffer count is 9 rather than the original 6 because this branch carries the merge with #59166, which added `input_ids`, `query_positions` and `is_padding` to the padded set.

## Test Plan

- [x] Write-equivalence on CPU: 468 shapes x 4 widths x 9 buffers, 0 mismatches
- [x] Write-equivalence **on device** at `num_reqs` 1 / 2 / 7 / 14 / 64 / 128 — identical
- [x] **CUDA graph capture and replay** at capture sizes 1 / 2 / 7 / 14, buffers overwritten between capture and replay so the replay must restore the padding. 4/4 pass.
- [x] `tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py` exercises the real launch path through `propose()` at `max_num_tokens=4096`, which makes the pad loop run four iterations. At the original 16-token shape it ran once and the loop stride was never exercised.
- [x] `ruff check` / `ruff format` / pre-commit clean

You're right, and the mechanism check confirms it — I'll move to the one-launch variant.

**Your diagnosis is correct and mine was wrong.** `BLOCK_SIZE = min(256, next_power_of_2(max_tokens_per_req))`, and at decode `max_tokens_per_req` is `k+1`, so:

| spec | BLOCK_SIZE | pad span 16384 | iterations in one program |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 4 | 16384 | 4096 |
| 7 | 8 | 16384 | **2048** |

A 1024-wide constexpr makes that 16. The failing (H100) Fault Tolerance E2E job is unrelated to this change.

It fails in test_worker_kill_survivor_unhealthy_and_dead_rejects_retry with psutil.ZombieProcess, in the test harness's own teardown — the test deliberately kills a worker, then inspects the PID. This is deterministic, not flaky: 7 consecutive retries, identical failure.

It is pulled in by an over-broad path dependency — .buildkite/test_areas/fault_tolerance.yaml lists vllm/v1/worker/, so a change to vllm/v1/worker/gpu/spec_decode/dflash/speculator.py triggers the whole fault-tolerance suite.

The same PR content passed this job on an earlier base (d7fc97a5c5) and fails on the current one, with no change to the diff — so it tracks the base, not this PR.

hey @fululi12  this looks good to me, the robot claimed an issue with your test itself, can you take a look to see if it's valid for you?
```
The new test only launches a one-program grid, so the PR's grid/offset arithmetic has no in-tree coverage · 
tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py (new test, docstring + shape); _run_prepare fixes max_num_reqs=4, max_num_tokens=16

At the test shape (num_reqs=1, nq=S=3, max_num_reqs=4, max_num_tokens=16):

pad_span = max(4+1-1, (4-1)*3, 16-3) = max(4, 9, 13) = 13
PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = min(1024, next_pow2(13)) = 16
grid = cdiv(13, 16) = 1
So tl.program_id(0) is always 0. The test cannot tell the correct offs = pid*BLOCK + arange apart from a regression such as offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE) (dropped program_id), a grid of (1,), or cdiv replaced by //. With any of those, production at max_num_tokens=16384 would leave query_slot_mapping[1024:16384] stale. Stale slots there would be real slot IDs from the target's previous step, and a larger graph replay could write draft K/V into them. This is the exact failure the padding exists to prevent.

The docstring says "every buffer has a tail wider than one block". That was true against the main kernel's block (8). It is false against PAD_BLOCK_SIZE (16), which is the block that now matters.

Fix: Add a max_num_tokens (and ideally max_num_reqs) kwarg to _run_prepare, and run the padding test at e.g. max_num_tokens=4096. That gives grid = 4 blocks of 1024 and covers the program_id path. Then assert the full tail, as the test already does. Correct the docstring sentence.
```

Thanks @dllehr-amd — I checked it, and the finding is **valid**. Fixed in `ab45a62869`.

**Confirmed.** At the shape the test used (`num_reqs=1, nq=S=3, max_num_reqs=4, max_num_tokens=16`):

```
pad_span       = max(4+1-1, (4-1)*3, 16-3) = 13
PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = min(1024, next_power_of_2(13)) = 16
grid           = cdiv(13, 16) = 1
```

So `tl.program_id(0)` was always 0, and

```python
offs = tl.program_id(0) * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
```

is then *identically* `tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)` — the test could not distinguish them, nor a grid hardcoded to `(1,)`. In production (`max_num_tokens=16384`, a 16-program grid) that regression leaves `query_slot_mapping[1024:]` holding real slot IDs from the target’’s previous step, which is exactly what this padding exists to prevent.

The docstring was also wrong: it claimed "every buffer has a tail wider than one block", true against the main kernel’’s block (8) but false against `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE` (16). Corrected.

**Fix** — the suggested one: `max_num_reqs`/`max_num_tokens` are now `_run_prepare` kwargs, and the padding test runs at `max_num_tokens=4096`:

```
pad_span = 4093, PAD_BLOCK_SIZE = 1024, grid = 4   -> program_id(0) takes 4 distinct values
```

so dropping the program offset now writes only the first block and fails. The tail assertion derives its length rather than hardcoding 13.

**One correction to the report:** `cdiv` replaced by `//` *was* already caught — `13 // 16 == 0` launches a zero-program grid, nothing is written, and the buffers keep the `-1`/`-2` sentinels `_run_prepare` pre-fills, so the existing assertions fail. The two real gaps were the dropped `program_id` and a hardcoded `(1,)` grid.

```python
tl.store(out_input_ids_ptr + block, 0, mask=mask)
tl.store(out_query_positions_ptr + block, 0, mask=mask)
tl.store(out_is_padding_ptr + block, True, mask=mask)
```

That fix went into `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel`, which is exactly the block this PR moves out into `_pad_dflash_buffers_kernel`. Thanks for finding this padding loop. On current `main` (79d0899cca), `_prepare_dflash_inputs_kernel` already pads with `BLOCK_SIZE = 128`, so the 2048-iteration case no longer occurs, and we measured only a small device-time change from this PR on GB200 (verify batch, 8 query tokens/request, `max_num_reqs` 256; device time from a CUDA graph of 20 calls, host time from eager calls):

| max_num_batched_tokens | reqs | device: main / this PR / alt (µs) | host: main / this PR / alt (µs) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16384 | 1 | 8.52 / 8.31 / 2.11 | 32.3 / 34.0 / 33.1 |
| 16384 | 32 | 7.89 / 8.17 / 2.12 | 31.9 / 34.2 / 31.7 |
| 8192 | 1 | 5.81 / 5.57 / 2.09 | 31.4 / 33.3 / 31.8 |
| 8192 | 32 | 5.28 / 5.17 / 2.09 | 31.8 / 33.5 / 32.3 |

"alt" keeps a single launch but adds 32 extra programs to the grid that split the padding loops between them, so host cost stays at main's level and device time drops to ~2.1 µs regardless of batch size. All three variants write identical buffers. I opened it as #65488 with you as co-author; happy to fold it into this PR instead if you prefer.

@WoosukKwon Thanks for measuring this properly -- and for the co-author credit on #65488.

**Your read is right, and I can point at where it changed.** `BLOCK_SIZE` was
`min(256, triton.next_power_of_2(max(1, max_tokens_per_req)))` until #63819
(`458334f00f`) pinned it to `128`. That formula is what this PR was written
against: at spec 7 it evaluates to 8, so the padding loops -- which span
`max_num_reqs`, not `max_tokens_per_req` -- walked a 16384-token span 8 elements
at a time in a single program. With `BLOCK_SIZE` pinned at 128 that's 16
iterations, which is exactly what this PR was trying to buy. The premise is
stale, and so is the comment in my own diff that still cites the old formula.

**Your numbers match that**, and I don't think this PR should land: device time
is a wash (8.52 -> 8.31, 7.89 -> 8.17) and host time is consistently ~2 us
worse. The alt is better on both axes, and better structurally -- splitting the
span across `NUM_PAD_PROGRAMS` means the per-program iteration count stays
bounded no matter what `BLOCK_SIZE` is later re-tuned to, whereas a separate
`PAD_BLOCK_SIZE` only decouples the two constants without parallelising the
work. Please go ahead with #65488; I'll close this one.

**One thing #65488 might want from here: the test.**
`tests/v1/spec_decode/test_dflash_prepare_inputs.py` asserts the padded tail
through the real `propose()` path rather than against a local copy of the loop

reference to `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE` in the assertions -- so it applies to your version

**If you take it, raise `max_num_tokens` to 16384.** Your stride is
`NUM_PAD_PROGRAMS * BLOCK_SIZE` = 4096, so at the 4096 the test currently uses

it's four iterations per program and the tail is covered. Happy to push that as
a PR against your branch if it's easier.

Closing in favour of **#65488**, which fixes the same padding cost in a better
way: it splits the padding span across `NUM_PAD_PROGRAMS` extra programs of the
same launch, so device time drops to ~2.1 us and stays flat in batch size,
while host cost stays at `main`'s level. This PR's separate `PAD_BLOCK_SIZE`
decoupled the two constants but left the padding serial in one program, and on

on host.

The original premise is also no longer current: #63819 (`458334f00f`) pinned
`BLOCK_SIZE` to `128`, replacing
`min(256, triton.next_power_of_2(max(1, max_tokens_per_req)))`, so the

The equivalence test here
